title: Terraform basics: state, plan and apply
objectives: Explain what `resource`, `data`, `variable`, `module` and `output` blocks each do, and choose `data` for something you read but don't own
Explain why state lives in a locked remote backend, one per environment, and is changed through Terraform rather than by editing the file
Read a plan: tell an in-place update from a replacement, predict the add/change/destroy line, and recognise drift and what `-refresh-only` does about it
Rename a resource with a `moved` block and adopt an existing object with an `import` block instead of destroying and recreating it
Write a check over `terraform show -json` output that summarises a plan and flags every change that deletes an object

questions.prompt: Your service needs the ID of a VPC that the network team manages in their own Terraform. Which block gives you its attributes **without** making the VPC yours?

options.text: `data "aws_vpc" "shared" { … }` — a read; nothing in your configuration will ever change or destroy it
`resource "aws_vpc" "shared" { … }` with the same settings, then read its `id`
An `import` block pointing at the VPC's ID
A `module` block whose `source` is the network team's repository

questions.explanation: A data source looks an object up and exposes its attributes; Terraform never creates, updates or destroys what it points at. A `resource` block declares an object *you* own — with no state entry it would create a second VPC. An `import` block is the opposite of what you want: it adopts the VPC into your state, after which your plans can modify or destroy it. Calling the network team's code as a module would create its resources all over again in your state.

questions.prompt: There's no remote backend, and the only `terraform.tfstate` gets deleted. The real objects are untouched. What does the next `terraform plan` propose?

options.text: Creating every resource again — Terraform no longer knows those objects are its own
No changes — it rediscovers the objects by querying the provider
Destroying the objects it can no longer find in state
An error: plan refuses to run without a state file

questions.explanation: State is the only link between an address like `random_pet.server` and the real object's ID. With it gone, every resource looks new — a real run printed `Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.` for two objects that still existed. Against a cloud API that plan either fails on a name clash or builds duplicates. Terraform can't "rediscover" ownership by matching settings, and it can't destroy objects it has no record of. That's why state belongs in a versioned remote backend.

questions.prompt: Two CI jobs run `terraform apply` against the same S3 backend with `use_lockfile = true`, a few seconds apart, with default flags. What happens to the second job?

options.text: It stops with *Error acquiring the state lock*; `-lock-timeout` defaults to `0s`, so it doesn't wait
It waits until the first apply finishes, then plans and applies
Both apply, and whichever finishes last overwrites the state
It applies on top of the first job's in-progress state

questions.explanation: Terraform locks state for every operation that could write it, and "if state locking fails, Terraform does not continue". Waiting is opt-in: `-lock-timeout=5m` retries for five minutes. "Both apply" is what you risk with no locking at all — which is the S3 backend's default, since `use_lockfile` defaults to `false`. In CI, serialise runs per state (a concurrency group) so the lock is a safety net, not the normal path.

questions.prompt: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main"` and one attribute marked `# forces replacement`. What will `apply` do?

options.text: Destroy the database and create a new one with a new identity — its data goes with the old instance unless you've arranged a restore
Modify the database in place; `-/+` is how a plan marks a large change
Create the new database, copy the data across, then destroy the old one
Nothing yet — a replacement only happens if you also pass `-replace`

questions.explanation: `-/+` reads "destroy and then create replacement": the provider can't change that attribute on a live object. `~` is the in-place symbol. Terraform never migrates data — even with `create_before_destroy` (shown as `+/-`) it only changes the order, creating a new, separate object first. `-replace=ADDR` forces a replacement Terraform wouldn't otherwise plan; it isn't needed to carry out one it already planned.

questions.prompt: A plan replaces one database and updates the tags on one security group. Which summary line does Terraform print?

options.text: `Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.`
`Plan: 0 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy.`
`Plan: 1 to add, 2 to change, 1 to destroy.`
`Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.`

questions.explanation: The summary counts objects: a replacement destroys one and creates one, so it adds 1 to *add* and 1 to *destroy*, and *change* is only the in-place tag update. The tempting `2 to change` is how a skimming reviewer reads it — and why a replaced database hides in plain sight. A real plan with two replacements and one update printed `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.`

questions.prompt: Someone hand-edited an object and you want to keep their change. You run `terraform apply -refresh-only`, and change nothing else. What does the next normal `plan` propose?

options.text: Undoing the edit again — the configuration still declares the old value
No changes — state now matches reality
An error, because state and configuration disagree
Nothing; `-refresh-only` also rewrote the `.tf` file to match

questions.explanation: `-refresh-only` updates **state** to match reality and never touches the configuration. A normal plan compares configuration with reality, so it still proposes to put the configured value back — the real run proposed recreating the hand-edited file straight after the refresh-only apply. To keep an outside change, edit the configuration to match; the plan is then empty.

questions.prompt: You rename `aws_db_instance.main` to `aws_db_instance.primary` in the code and change nothing else. What does the next plan propose, and what's the fix?

options.text: Destroy `main` and create `primary`; fix it with a `moved` block whose `from` is `aws_db_instance.main` and `to` is `aws_db_instance.primary`
No changes — Terraform matches the object by its settings, not its name
An in-place rename (`~`), which is safe to apply
Destroy and create; fix it with an `import` block for `primary`

questions.explanation: State is keyed by address, so a new name is a new resource and the old address has no configuration: `Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.` A `moved` block (Terraform 1.1+) tells Terraform the object at the old address now lives at the new one, and the plan becomes *"has moved to"* with nothing to add or destroy. An `import` block is for objects Terraform doesn't manage yet; this one is already in state under `main`, which would still be destroyed.

questions.prompt: Staging and production should share Terraform code, and the staging CI role must not be able to touch production. Which layout do Terraform's docs point to?

options.text: Shared modules plus one small root module per environment, each with its own backend and credentials
One configuration with `staging` and `production` CLI workspaces
One configuration and one state, with `count = var.env == "production" ? 1 : 0` on each resource
A long-lived git branch per environment, each applied from its own branch

questions.explanation: CLI workspaces give one configuration several states *in the same backend*, so the same credentials reach all of them — the docs say they are "not a suitable isolation mechanism" when deployments need separate credentials and access controls. The documented alternative is reusable modules plus a root module per deployment that holds only a backend block and a few `module` calls. One shared state puts both environments in one blast radius, and per-environment branches drift apart because the change you tested is never the change you merge.

questions.prompt: In `terraform show -json` output, a change has `"actions": ["create", "delete"]`. What is it?

options.text: A replacement with `create_before_destroy`: the new object is created, then the old one destroyed
Two different resources — one being created and one being destroyed
A create that Terraform will roll back if it fails
An in-place update, written as a create and a delete

questions.explanation: Each entry in `resource_changes` is one resource instance, and the documented `actions` values include two spellings of replace: `["delete", "create"]` (the default order) and `["create", "delete"]` (with `create_before_destroy`). An update is `["update"]`, and Terraform has no automatic rollback. The format writes replacements this way, the reference says, so that a caller can scan for `"delete"` and catch every plan that deletes something — reading only `actions[0]` misses this one.

prompts.prompt: Read a VPC you don't own, and expose its ID as an output.
prompts.explanation: A data source is declared with `data` and referenced with a `data.` prefix — `data.aws_vpc.shared.id` — which keeps reads visibly separate from `aws_vpc.shared`, a VPC you'd own. An `output` is how a value leaves a module (or is printed after apply).

prompts.prompt: Keep production state in S3 with S3-native locking turned on (generally available since Terraform 1.11).
prompts.explanation: The `backend` block lives inside `terraform { }` and is read before anything else, so it can't use variables. Locking on the S3 backend is opt-in — `use_lockfile` defaults to `false` — and the older `dynamodb_table` locking is deprecated.

prompts.prompt: Save a plan, turn it into JSON for a CI check, then apply exactly the plan that was checked.
prompts.explanation: `-out` writes a saved plan; `terraform show -json` renders it in the documented JSON format; `apply tfplan` performs those actions without re-planning or prompting — and refuses with *Saved plan is stale* if the state changed in between. The plan file holds variable values in clear text, so treat it like state.

prompts.prompt: Rename the database's address without destroying it.
prompts.explanation: `moved` (Terraform 1.1+) records that the object bound to `from` now belongs to `to`, so the plan shows *"has moved to"* instead of a destroy and a create. Keep the block around: removing it later is a breaking change for any configuration that hasn't applied the move yet.

prompts.prompt: Adopt a bucket that was created by hand (Terraform 1.5+). A matching `resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets"` block already exists.
prompts.explanation: `to` is the address in your configuration; `id` is the provider's identifier for the real object (for an S3 bucket, its name). The plan shows *"will be imported"*, state changes at apply, and once the address is in state the block is a no-op you may delete or keep as a record.

code: # In CI, with no -var, no .tfvars file and no TF_VAR_env set:
snippets.question: What does the plan do?
snippets.answer: It fails: Error: No value for required variable
snippets.explanation: A variable with no default is required. Interactively, `plan` would prompt for it; with `-input=false`, as in CI, Terraform stops with *No value for required variable — the root module input variable "env" is not set, and has no default value*. It doesn't fall back to an empty string. That's the behaviour you want for an environment name: give it no default, so a pipeline that forgot to set it can't quietly plan against the wrong environment.

code: keepers = { env = var.env }   # changing a keeper forces a new pet
input = { env = var.env, replicas = 2 }   # updates in place
# Applied with the default. Now: terraform plan -var env=production
snippets.question: What is the plan's summary line?
snippets.answer: Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.
acceptable: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy
snippets.explanation: The pet is replaced because a keeper changed, and the file is replaced because its content embeds the pet's new name — replacement spreads through references. `terraform_data.config` is the only in-place update. Each replacement is one destroy plus one create, so two replacements and one update give exactly the line Terraform 1.16 printed: `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.`

code: # Now the file says this instead, and nothing else changed:
snippets.question: What does the plan propose?
snippets.answer: Create random_pet.api and destroy random_pet.worker — Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
acceptable: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
destroy the old one and create a new one
snippets.explanation: State binds the real object to the address `random_pet.worker`. That address no longer has configuration (so: destroy), and `random_pet.api` has no object (so: create). Terraform doesn't match by settings, so for a database this rename is data loss. A `moved` block with `from = random_pet.worker` and `to = random_pet.api` turns it into `Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.`

code: # The real object was created earlier with min = 8000, max = 8999 (result 8443).
max = 9999      # differs from the real object; changing max forces replacement
snippets.question: What is the summary line?
snippets.answer: Plan: 1 to import, 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
acceptable: 1 to import, 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy
import it, then destroy and recreate it
snippets.explanation: Import adopts the existing object, then the plan reconciles it with the configuration like any other resource — and `max` can't change in place, so the object you meant to adopt is replaced. Terraform even prints `# Warning: this will destroy the imported resource`. Make the configuration match the real object first, import with an empty diff, and change it in a later plan. In JSON this is one change with `actions: ["delete", "create"]` **and** an `importing` object.
